name: Bhee ji Bhaji
subtitle: dry-cooked lotus stem, crisp at the edges and sharp with amchur

ingredients.note: bhee — scrub the hollows out under running water
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Peel the lotus stem and slice it, then wash the rounds twice — the hollow channels hold silt that no amount of cooking will remove.
Slice evenly at 5mm. Thicker rounds stay woody in the middle while the thin ones fall apart.
Have everything chopped before you start; once the bhee is parboiled the dish moves quickly.

steps.text: Pressure cook the lotus stem rounds with the water and 1/2 tsp salt for 8 minutes, about 2 whistles, then drain and reserve 1/4 cup of the cooking water.
steps.tip: Bhee is stubborn. Test a round — it should give under a fork but still hold its shape, never mash.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pan and crackle the ajwain and cumin for 30 seconds.
Add the asafoetida, then the crushed garlic, and fry 45 seconds until it turns pale gold.
Add the onion, ginger and green chilli, and fry 7 minutes until the onion is golden at the edges.
Add the tomato, turmeric, chilli powder and coriander powder, and cook 6 minutes until the tomato collapses and the oil separates.
Tip in the drained lotus stem and toss to coat every round in masala.
Add the reserved cooking water, cover, and cook 8 minutes over low heat.
Uncover, raise the heat and fry 6-8 minutes without stirring much, until the rounds catch and brown in patches.
steps.tip: The browned edges are the whole point of a bhaji. Stir every 2 minutes at most, or nothing will colour.

steps.text: Sprinkle over the amchur and salt, toss once, and take off the heat.
steps.tip: Amchur goes in at the end. Cooked long it turns flat and slightly bitter.

steps.text: Finish with coriander leaves and serve with phulka.

storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. Reheat dry in a hot pan rather than a microwave so the edges crisp again.
